headline: The Legal & Immigration Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet a client, take their name, date of birth and phone number, ask simple intake questions, ask for documents politely, get help when you don't understand, and start Legal & Immigration Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet a client, say your name and role, and pronounce basic intake words clearly.
lessons.focus: Five pure vowels, ch, j, ll, rr, the written accent, and formal greetings

words.note: ll sounds like English y: a-pe-YI-do.
The accent marks the stressed syllable: te-LÉ-fo-no.
cc sounds like k + s; stress falls on the accented ó.
rr is a strong rolled r; one r between vowels is a quick tap.
j sounds like a strong English h; the h in hijos is silent.
Keep each vowel short and pure: o-fi-ci-na.
ch sounds like ch in church.

words.en: Good morning, my name is Laura and I'm a paralegal.
words.es: Buenos días, me llamo Laura y soy paralegal.

words.note: Formal usted: use it with every client.
Say bienvenido to a man.

words.en: See you later, see you at the appointment.
words.es: Hasta luego, nos vemos en la cita.

lessons.speaking: Greet a new client at the front desk, say your name and role, ask their name, and say goodbye until the appointment.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say dates, clock times, case numbers and fees, and count pages and copies with a client.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, dates, and counting pages, copies and dollars

words.note: Always write the ñ: año means year; without the tilde it is a different word.
Spanish gives the day first, then the month, then the year. US forms often put the month first, so check the order on each form.
Plural: los dólares.

words.en: The appointment is on Tuesday at 10:30.
words.es: La cita es el martes a las 10:30.
words.note: Use a las for clock times; for 1:00 say a la una.
You can also say son las nueve y cuarto.

words.en: Is your date of birth May 5, 1990?
words.es: ¿Su fecha de nacimiento es el 5 de mayo de 1990?
Su número de caso termina en 482.

lessons.speaking: Ask a client for their date of birth, then tell them the time of their next appointment and how many pages they will sign.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Use ser and estar to say who you are, where the office is, and how a client or a form is.
lessons.focus: ser for identity and importance, estar for location, feelings and readiness

words.note: Use estar: está listo. Lista for a feminine noun.
Mostly used with estar; casada for a woman.
Use ser: soy soltero. Soltera for a woman.
Use estar: está preocupada for a woman.
For a woman: la abogada.
Same word for a woman: la intérprete.
ser: who you are. Say this only if you are a licensed attorney; a paralegal says Soy paralegal. A man says soy su abogado.

words.en: The office is on the second floor.
words.es: La oficina está en el segundo piso.
words.note: estar for location.
Ask a man: ¿Está usted casado?

words.en: The form is ready to sign.
words.es: El formulario está listo para firmar.

lessons.speaking: Tell a client who you are, where the office is, and that the interpreter is here, then ask if they are married or single.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask what documents a client has, say what you need, and say what has to be done.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer, and hay que + infinitive for what must be done

words.note: Acta is feminine but takes el because it starts with a stressed a; plural las actas.
Short for la fotografía, so it is feminine.

words.en: There's a problem with the date.
words.es: Hay un problema con la fecha.
words.note: hay means there is or there are.

words.en: I need a copy of your birth certificate.
words.es: Necesito una copia de su acta de nacimiento.

words.en: The form has to be signed here.
words.es: Hay que firmar el formulario aquí.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something must be done, no specific person.

lessons.speaking: Ask a client if they have their passport and ID, say which certificate you need a copy of, and ask if they want an interpreter.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where a client will go, what you are going to do, and ask if they can come.
lessons.focus: ir and ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer for what someone does, poder for can

words.en: Tomorrow I'm going to call the court.
words.es: Mañana voy a llamar a la corte.

words.en: We're going to prepare everything together.
Can you come on Monday at 2?
According to the letter, you are going to speak with the judge.
words.es: Según la carta, usted va a hablar con la jueza.

words.en: What do you do at your job?
words.note: hacer: hago, hace, hacemos, hacen.

lessons.speaking: Tell a client what you are going to do tomorrow, ask if they can come on Monday, and tell them where the waiting room is.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Ask a client simple present-tense questions about home, work, family and language.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs: hablo, vive, leemos, estudian, llamas

words.note: Common in Mexican and US Spanish; feminine: la patrona.
Ends in -a but is masculine: el idioma.

words.es: Yo hablo un poco de español.

words.en: Do you live with your family?
Do your children go to school here?
We read every page with you.
words.es: Nosotros leemos cada página con usted.

words.en: Are you calling the client today?
words.note: tú with a coworker; use a before a person as the object.

lessons.speaking: Ask a client who they live with, whether they work, and which language they understand, then say you speak a little Spanish.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask basic intake questions about origin, address, arrival, household and children.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál with rising ¿…?

words.note: Plural: ¿quiénes? for more than one person.
Agrees with the noun: cuánto tiempo, cuántos hijos, cuántas veces.
Two words for why; porque, one word, means because.
Use ¿Cuál es…? for name, address and phone number.

words.en: When did you arrive in the United States?
words.note: llegó is past tense; learn it as a set question.

words.en: How many children do you have?
How can we help you today?

lessons.speaking: Ask a client where they are from, what their current address is, who lives with them and how many children they have.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what a client does not have to do, what is still pending, and ask for more or another copy.
lessons.focus: Negatives no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, and más, menos, otro

words.note: Keep no before the verb: no firmo nada.
Never put un before it: otra copia, not una otra copia.

words.en: You don't have to sign anything today.
words.es: Usted no tiene que firmar nada hoy.
words.note: Say this only if the attorney has confirmed it.

words.en: We don't have an answer yet.
The attorney never ignores a court letter.
words.es: La abogada nunca ignora una carta de la corte.
No hay nada de malo en preguntar.

lessons.speaking: Tell a client there is no answer yet, that they don't have to sign anything today, and ask if they need more time.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask a client politely to sit, wait, sign, write and bring papers using ¿Puede…? and usted commands.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede + infinitive? and usted commands: firme, tome, escriba, traiga, espere, ponga

words.note: Mexican and US Spanish; many countries say el bolígrafo.
Formal usted command from tomar.

words.en: Write your name on this line.
words.es: Escriba su nombre en esta línea.

words.en: Bring the originals to the next appointment.
words.es: Traiga los originales a la próxima cita.
words.note: Irregular command from traer: traiga.

words.es: Espere aquí un momento, por favor.

words.en: Put the papers in this envelope.
words.es: Ponga los papeles en este sobre.
words.note: Irregular command from poner: ponga.

lessons.speaking: Ask a client to sit down, write their name on the line, sign the form, and bring the originals to the next appointment.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize legal cognates and ask a client to repeat, slow down or wait for an interpreter.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente, and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.
For a woman: la residente.
For a woman: la agente.

words.en: I don't understand, can you explain it to me again?
words.es: No entiendo, ¿me lo puede explicar otra vez?

words.en: One moment, I'm going to call the interpreter.
words.es: Un momento, voy a llamar al intérprete.
words.note: a + el = al before a person as the object.

words.en: How do you say 'hearing' in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Tell a client your Spanish is basic, ask them to repeat more slowly, and say you are going to call the interpreter.
